grammar.title: Nominalisation in Formal English
grammar.explanation:
**Nominalisation** means expressing an action or quality as a **noun** instead of a verb or adjective. *Prices rose sharply* becomes *there was **a sharp rise in** prices*.

It is typical of academic, business and news writing. It packs more information into fewer words and sounds more objective, which is why reports speak of the **suppression** of protests or a **reduction** in carbon dioxide emissions.

Two things change: the verb becomes a noun, and the **adverb becomes an adjective**. *The company expanded rapidly* becomes *the company's **rapid expansion***.

Common endings include **-tion / -sion** (*decide → decision*), **-ment** (*develop → development*), **-ance / -ence** (*important → importance*), **-ity** (*possible → possibility*) and **-ness** (*aware → awareness*). Some nouns keep the verb's form: *rise, fall, change, growth*.

Each noun takes a fixed preposition. Use **in** for changes (*a rise **in** prices*), **on** for effects (*an effect **on** wildlife*), **for** for demand and reasons (*a demand **for** change*), **to** for solutions and access (*a solution **to** the problem*), and **of** for causes and analysis (*the cause **of** the damage*).

For the amount of a change, use **of**: *an increase **of** five percent*, but *an increase **in** emissions*. Do not overdo nominalisation, or a text becomes heavy and hard to read.
examples: *There has been **a sharp rise in** unemployment.* (rise in)
*The new law will have **an effect on** small businesses.* (effect on)
*There is growing **awareness of** climate change.* (aware → awareness)
***The failure of** the talks surprised everyone.* (fail → failure)
*There is increasing **demand for** online courses.* (demand for)
***A careful analysis of** the data revealed a pattern.* (analyse → analysis)

practice.q: Rewrite with nominalisation: The government decided to end the ceasefire talks. (use decision)
practice.a: The government's decision to end the ceasefire talks surprised everyone.

practice.q: Rewrite with nominalisation: Carbon dioxide emissions rose sharply last year. (use a sharp rise in)
practice.a: There was a sharp rise in carbon dioxide emissions last year.

practice.q: Rewrite with nominalisation: People became more aware of the damage to the marshes. (use awareness of)
practice.a: There was growing awareness of the damage to the marshes.

practice.q: Rewrite with nominalisation: The storm affected the clammy coastal town badly. (use an effect on)
practice.a: The storm had a bad effect on the clammy coastal town.
